title: Operations Management Adventure 1: Production Methods
welcome_lead: Today you'll compare job, batch, flow and mass customisation production.
meta_desc: Business Management Ops: job, batch, flow and mass customisation production methods.
final_note: You compared four production methods and matched each to its ideal market.

walkthroughs.body_html:
One-off, made to order.

Examples: wedding cakes, tailored suits, custom yachts.

Strengths: highly customised, high price; Weaknesses: slow, expensive, labour-intensive.

Batch — groups of identical units (a bakery's loaves, then rolls). Some flexibility, switching cost between batches.

Flow — continuous, standardised, capital-intensive (car assembly line). Low unit cost from economies of scale, inflexible.

Mass customisation combines flow with personalisation via modular design.

Examples: Dell PCs, Nike custom trainers. Customers configure online, the firm assembles standard modules.

This blurs the line between job and flow — high variety at near-flow cost.

mcqs.q: Is flow production always the cheapest method per unit?
options: Quality control is outsourced to customers by law.
Flow production refers to manufacturing liquids only.
Only at high, steady volumes — its large set-up costs need scale to spread; at low volumes or with varied products, batch or job production can be cheaper.
Flow production lowers unit costs for any business.

mcqs.q: Does mass customisation mean every product is handmade?
options: Customised products must always be made by job production.
Flow production refers to manufacturing liquids only.
Mass customisation means customers assemble products themselves in store.
No — it uses flexible production technology to offer customised options at near mass-production costs, combining scale with variety.

mcqs.q: Is quality only the responsibility of inspectors?
options: Quality control is outsourced to customers by law.
Quality is checked by the quality department, so other workers needn't worry about it.
Mass customisation means customers assemble products themselves in store.
In a total quality management culture, every employee is responsible for quality at their own stage, aiming to prevent defects rather than catch them at the end.
